query: Consider a homogenized Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy initially possessing a dual-phase lamellar structure (FCC/B2) that is strong yet brittle due to stress concentration at incoherent interfaces. The goal is to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off. A hypothesis is proposed involving a High-Pressure and High-Temperature (HPHT) treatment using a hexahedron-anvil apparatus. Predict that applying approximately 6 GPa at 1473 K for 2 hours will induce a topological transformation of the lamellae into a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces. This structure is hypothesized to facilitate multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocation transfer, stacking faults, twinning) and homogeneous strain distribution, effectively arresting interfacial cracking. The mechanism relies on the coherent interface allowing dislocation transfer to alleviate stress. The boundary condition requires that the pressure and temperature are sufficient to induce this specific topological change but not so high as to cause phase instability. A discriminating measurement should compare the fracture surface morphology (isolated microcracks vs. elongated cracks) and the evolution of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities between the treated sample and the baseline, specifically checking if the GND densities of both phases converge at high strain. Falsification would involve showing that conventional thermal-mechanical treatments fail to produce the same hierarchical coherence or GND homogenization.

generation.structural_mediator: Hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces between FCC and B2 phases.
generation.mechanism: Coherent interfaces facilitate dislocation transfer between phases, alleviating stress concentrations and enabling multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocation transfer, stacking faults, twinning) that promote homogeneous strain distribution and arrest interfacial cracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significant improvement in ductility without sacrificing strength; fracture surface morphology shifts from isolated microcracks to elongated cracks; geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities of both FCC and B2 phases converge at high strain.
generation.baseline: As-cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy with incoherent FCC/B2 lamellar interfaces exhibiting high strength but low ductility due to stress concentration and interfacial cracking.
generation.boundary: HPHT parameters must remain within the window that induces coherent interface formation without triggering phase decomposition or instability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact pressure-temperature window for achieving coherent interfaces without phase instability is not precisely defined in existing literature; the convergence of GND densities may vary depending on strain rate and temperature during deformation.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform conventional thermal-mechanical treatments on the same alloy and demonstrate that they fail to produce the hierarchical coherent microstructure or the convergence of GND densities observed under HPHT treatment; alternatively, show that HPHT treatment at the specified conditions does not result in coherent interfaces or improved ductility.

cited_evidence.text: Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] . High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

To verify this novel alloy design strategy, an industrial scale AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared, as shown in Fig. 1a . The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. The coupled grown two phases showed a clear compositional contrast, with the regions marked by A in Fig. 2b were rich in Co, Cr and Fe, while the regions marked by B were rich in Al and Ni (detailed compositional information given in Table 1 ). An enlarged microstructure given in Fig. 2c shows that dense nanoscale NiAl-rich precipitates (marked as B II ) occurred in the CoCrFe-rich region. As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
